title: Joys and hopes (Gaudium et Spes 1)
hookLine: nothing genuinely human fails to echo in the hearts of Christ's followers
tomorrow: when every feed has an opinion, whose voice is left?

lines: A FLOOD ON THE KITCHEN TV.
THEN AN AD. THEN THE WEATHER.
cards: The kitchen TV is on low. A flood somewhere far away: brown water up to the porch roofs, a man wading with a dog in his arms. Then an ad for car insurance.
Then the weather. The sound of other people's disasters is part of the background hum of a weeknight, and it passes in seconds.
Vatican II's document on the Church in the modern world opens its very first sentence on that hum, and refuses to let it pass.

teach.b: The document is named for its first words, Gaudium et Spes: joy and hope. The sentence comes in four parts. First, the list: the joys and the hopes, the griefs and the anxieties of people today.
It doesn't stop at the happy half.

Second, who comes first: especially, the council says, those who are poor or in any way afflicted. Third, the turn. These, it says, are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ as well.
Theirs. Then the line the day hangs on: nothing genuinely human fails to raise an echo in their hearts. Fourth, the reason.
The Church, the paragraph says, is made of human beings, so it knows itself bound to the whole human race and its history.
Paul had put the instinct in one line to the Romans: "Rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep." And the next paragraph of the council's document widens the address on purpose.
It speaks not only to Catholics, but to all people.
The man wading with his dog belongs in that first sentence.

how: Catholics often quote the opening of Gaudium et Spes when speaking of the Church's care for the poor and suffering, and parishes bring the world's needs into the prayers of the faithful at Mass.

o: people's joys and griefs, taken as the Church's own
the good news the Church shares about itself
a feast day of celebration after a hard Lent

games.q: Gaudium et Spes 1 — tap the pairs.
p: these belong to Christ's followers too

s: 'joys and hopes' is a cheerful slogan about the Church's own good news
it's about people's joys and griefs, taken as the Church's own.
the opening list names grief and anxiety, not only joy and hope
joys, hopes, griefs and anxieties, with the poor named first.
Gaudium et Spes speaks only to Catholics
its second paragraph addresses all people.

games.q: your group chat goes from a friend's engagement photos to a fundraiser for a stranger whose house burned. someone types "not our problem, we don't know her." what would Gaudium et Spes 1 say?
o: only the engagement belongs; a stranger's fire isn't ours.
both belong: joys and griefs alike echo in Christ's followers.
only the fire belongs; celebrating is a distraction now.
games.why: the first sentence holds joys and hopes, griefs and anxieties together, the afflicted named first, and says nothing genuinely human fails to echo in Christ's followers.

practice: Let your ears go out past the room: traffic, a neighbor's TV, a bird, a pipe knocking. Choose one sound another person made, and stay with it, knowing there's a whole day behind it, a joy or a worry you'll never hear about.
If you pray, hold that unknown person in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Joys and hopes. The council's first words to the modern world: everyone's joys and griefs, taken as its own.

orig.note: Latin for joy and hope: the opening words that give the document its name.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing human is foreign. The flood far away is close enough to echo. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World
